headline: Open 180B model leads 10 Hugging Face leaderboards with Zero-Token Confidence judge
summary: Darwin-180B-RSI excels in real-world tasks like document parsing and structured output, surpassing previous academic benchmarks. It achieves this with a novel Zero-Token Confidence (ZTC) judge.
details: An open 180B parameter model, Darwin-180B-RSI, has achieved the top position in 10 official Hugging Face benchmarks. This includes leading in tests with the most competitors, such as MMLU-Pro (141 models) and GPQA (111 models).

Crucially, the model excels not just in academic "exam-type" tests, but also in new benchmarks measuring real-world enterprise tasks. These include multilingual document parsing, valid JSON/YAML output generation, and structured field extraction.

Darwin-180B-RSI scored 83.65% in MDPBench for multilingual document parsing, a critical step for RAG systems. It also achieved 98.95% in Liquid AI's IFStruct for valid JSON/YAML output and 90.29% in LlamaIndex's ExtractBench for structured PDF extraction.

These real-world performance metrics are vital for AI agent pipelines, where model output is read by code, not humans. Errors in data types, keys, or parsing can halt entire automated processes, making precision paramount.

The model, Darwin-180B-RSI, is built upon Alibaba's open Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model. Its enhanced performance is attributed to a proprietary Model-level Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) technique, where the model learns from its own verified successes.

A key innovation is Zero-Token Confidence (ZTC), an internal mechanism that calculates the probability of a response being correct by reading the model's internal state. This eliminates the need for additional tokens or external AI judges.

ZTC offers an alternative to traditional external AI judges, which generate additional text to evaluate responses. By using zero additional tokens, ZTC provides an efficient way for AI agents to filter incorrect actions before execution.

Hugging Face recognized the agent evaluation strategy using ZTC in Gate Arcade, selecting it as one of their "Spaces of the Week." Gate Arcade demonstrates how ZTC can improve agent decision-making by retaining incorrect actions.

headline_marked: [[LLM self-hosting costs cut by 10x]] with continuous batching, boosting GPU utilization
headline: LLM self-hosting costs cut by 10x with continuous batching, boosting GPU utilization
summary: GPU rental price is fixed, but cost per million tokens isn't. Continuous batching can reduce LLM self-hosting costs by over 10x by maximizing GPU utilization, turning $20/M tokens into $1.
details: Self-hosting an open-weight LLM is often expensive due to low GPU utilization, not the GPU's hourly rental price. Continuous batching and honest utilization numbers can shift the true cost per million tokens by more than 10x. This post provides a model and key server settings to optimize costs.

The hourly price of an accelerator is an input, not the answer to token cost. Throughput, which depends on the GPU, model, request pattern, and server configuration, is the crucial conversion factor between GPU-seconds and tokens. Two identical GPUs can have vastly different unit economics.

A naive server processes requests sequentially, leaving the GPU idle between prefill and decode steps. Continuous batching, popularized by vLLM, keeps multiple sequences in-flight, injecting new requests as slots free up. This iteration-level scheduling significantly boosts aggregate throughput.

Illustrative simulations show that moving from one to a few dozen in-flight requests can reduce the price per million tokens from $20 to around $1. The curve flattens when a bottleneck is hit, typically the KV-cache memory rather than raw compute power.

The KV cache stores keys and values for all previous tokens, growing with context length and batch size. When it fills, new requests are queued or preempted, limiting concurrency. Quantization, like 4-bit GGUF, frees up this memory, allowing for higher concurrency and cost reduction when combined with batching.

Quantization does not reliably cut costs on an already underutilized GPU. Its benefit comes from enabling more concurrency. Running GGUF on a CPU is a different trade-off, viable for low-traffic internal tools where a GPU would sit idle, but GPUs win decisively for higher traffic volumes.

Accurate cost modeling requires four inputs, three of which are measurable. It's crucial to benchmark with your own input/output length distribution, as vendor benchmarks with high batch sizes and short outputs can be misleading. Output-heavy workloads have lower tokens-per-hour and higher costs.
caption:
